summary: Defines MIB objects for managing uninterruptible power supply (UPS) systems. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 1628 lists the values a network management program can read and set on an uninterruptible power supply. It covers the battery, the power coming in, the power going out, the bypass, and a list of named alarms such as on battery, low battery and fan failure.

what alarms can a ups raise
subtitle: The SNMP objects that let a manager watch and control an uninterruptible power supply.

tldr.problem: Network managers could not tell, over SNMP, whether the battery under a rack was healthy, which way the power was flowing, or why the UPS had switched to bypass.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 1628 defines nine groups of managed objects for uninterruptible power supplies, covering identification, batteries, input, output, bypass, alarms, tests, control and configuration, plus four notifications.
tldr.outcome: It is a document that defines objects rather than a protocol, and it has not been obsoleted or updated. Its Security Considerations section says only that security issues are not discussed in it.

today: RFC 1628 is an Informational RFC that defines a portion of the Management Information Base, and it has not been obsoleted or updated. Its Security Considerations section says only that security issues are not discussed in it.

sections.title: What the Memo Defines
sections.content:
RFC 1628 defines a portion of the Management Information Base for use with network management protocols in the Internet community, and in particular it defines objects for managing uninterruptible power supply, UPS, systems. The overview says the same thing in fewer words: it defines the managed objects for uninterruptible power supplies that are to be manageable via the Simple Network Management Protocol.

The module is rooted at upsMIB ::= { mib-2 33 }, alongside the other managed objects of the Internet, and its contents divide under upsObjects ::= { upsMIB 1 } into nine groups: the device identification group at { upsObjects 1 }, the battery group at 2, the input group at 3, the output group at 4, the bypass group at 5, the alarm group at 6, the test group at 7, the control group at 8 and the configuration group at 9. A separate branch, upsTraps ::= { upsMIB 2 }, holds the well-known notifications that UPS agents send.

Two new data types are defined for the module. PositiveInteger is a non-zero and non-negative value, written as INTEGER from 1 to 2147483647, and NonNegativeInteger is a non-negative value, INTEGER from 0 to 2147483647. Both are textual conventions, which the memo uses for convenience without changing how the underlying values are encoded.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo adds a standard set of values to the tree of things a network manager can read. The values are grouped by what they describe: the battery, the incoming power, the outgoing power, the bypass, alarms, tests, controls and settings.

sections.title: The SNMPv2 Network Management Framework
sections.content:
The framework the objects live in has four major components. RFC 1442 defines the SMI, the mechanisms used for describing and naming objects for the purpose of management. STD 17, RFC 1213, defines MIB-II, the core set of managed objects for the Internet suite of protocols. RFC 1445 defines the administrative and other architectural aspects of the framework. RFC 1448 defines the protocol used for network access to managed objects.

The framework permits new objects to be defined for the purpose of experimentation and evaluation, which is the door this module walks through.

The object definitions themselves follow the same pattern as any other MIB. Managed objects are accessed through a virtual information store, the Management Information Base, and objects in it are defined using the subset of Abstract Syntax Notation One defined in the SMI. Each object type is named by an OBJECT IDENTIFIER, an administratively assigned name, and the object type together with an object instance serves to uniquely identify a specific instantiation of the object. For human convenience a textual string, termed the descriptor, is often used to refer to the object type.
sections.plainLanguage: The objects follow the same rules as every other managed object on the network: each one has a numeric name in a tree, a type, and a set of permissions saying whether a manager may read it, write it or only discover that it exists.

sections.title: Identification and Batteries
sections.content:
The device identification group holds six objects, and the memo notes that all of them except two are set at device initialisation and remain static. upsIdentManufacturer is the name of the UPS manufacturer and upsIdentModel is the model designation, both read-only. upsIdentUPSSoftwareVersion is the UPS firmware or software version and upsIdentAgentSoftwareVersion is the version of the management agent itself; the memo warns that the two may or may not hold the same value in some implementations. The two writable objects are upsIdentName, a string identifying the UPS, and upsIdentAttachedDevices, a string identifying the devices attached to the outputs, and the memo says both should be set by the administrator.

The battery group starts with upsBatteryStatus, an enumeration with four values: unknown, batteryNormal, batteryLow and batteryDepleted. The meanings are defined against another object, upsConfigLowBattTime: a value of batteryNormal means the remaining run-time is greater than that setting, batteryLow means it is less than or equal to it, and batteryDepleted means the UPS will be unable to sustain the present load if the utility power is lost, including the possibility that the power is already absent and the UPS cannot sustain the output.

The rest of the group measures the battery directly. upsSecondsOnBattery is the elapsed time since the UPS last switched to battery power, or the time since the management subsystem was last restarted, whichever is less, and zero is returned if the unit is not on battery power. upsEstimatedMinutesRemaining is an estimate of the time to depletion under the present load if the utility power is lost and stays lost, and upsEstimatedChargeRemaining is the same idea as a percentage of full charge. Finally there are three measurements: upsBatteryVoltage in tenths of a volt, upsBatteryCurrent in tenths of an amp, and upsBatteryTemperature in degrees Centigrade, the ambient temperature at or near the battery casing.
sections.plainLanguage: The battery group answers the questions an operator actually asks: is it on battery, how long is left, how full is it, and what is the temperature. The low battery warning is defined against a configurable threshold rather than a fixed number of minutes.

sections.title: Power In, Power Out and Bypass
sections.content:
The input group describes the power arriving from the utility. upsInputLineBads counts how many times the input entered an out-of-tolerance condition as defined by the manufacturer, incremented each time the input moves from no lines out of tolerance to one or more. upsInputNumLines gives the number of input lines the device uses and says how many rows the input table has. The table itself has one row per line, with upsInputLineIndex, the frequency, the voltage in RMS volts, the current in tenths of an RMS amp, and the true power in watts.

The output group describes what the UPS is delivering. Its first object, upsOutputSource, is an enumeration of seven values: other, none, normal, bypass, battery, booster and reducer. It reports the present source of output power, and the memo explains that none means there is no source of output power at all, for example because the system has opened the output breaker. The group also holds the output frequency, the number of output lines used, and an output table with one row per line giving the line index, the voltage, the current, the power and the percentage load.

The bypass group is the third of the three electrical groups. It carries upsBypassFrequency, the number of bypass lines the device uses, and a bypass table with a row per line giving the line index, the frequency, the voltage and the current, together with the age and hold time of each entry.
sections.plainLanguage: Three groups cover the electricity: what is coming in, what is going out, and what the bypass path is doing. The most useful single value is the source of the output, because it says at a glance whether the load is on the utility, on the battery, or on the bypass.

sections.title: Alarms, Tests and Control
sections.content:
The alarm group keeps a table of the conditions that are currently in effect. upsAlarmsPresent is the present number of active alarm conditions, and the table holds zero, one or many rows depending on how many conditions apply. The agent creates a row when a condition is detected and deletes it when the condition no longer applies, starting with an identifier of 1 and incrementing it each time a row is created, wrapping to the first free value at or above 1 when the maximum would be exceeded. The memo warns that the table may therefore become sparse, that entries should not be assumed to be in chronological order because the identifier might have wrapped, and that no two rows may have the same description, since alarms define conditions.

Each row holds three values: an identifier, a description given as an AutonomousType, that is an OBJECT IDENTIFIER, and the time the alarm was raised. Using an identifier for the description lets one table carry both the well-known alarms and any an implementation defines in its own private enterprise MIB. The memo lists twenty-four well-known alarms, including battery bad, on battery, low battery, depleted battery, temperature bad, input bad, output bad, output overload, on bypass, bypass bad, output off as requested, UPS off as requested, charger failed, UPS output off, UPS system off, fan failure, fuse failure, general fault, diagnostic test failed, communications lost, awaiting power, shutdown pending, shutdown imminent and test in progress.

Four notifications are defined for the agents to send. upsTrapOnBattery carries the estimated minutes remaining, the seconds on battery and the low battery threshold. upsTrapTestCompleted reports that a test has finished. upsTrapAlarmEntryAdded and upsTrapAlarmEntryRemoved report that an alarm has come or gone. The memo attaches a caution to the whole set: care must be taken to ensure that no particular notification is sent to a single receiving entity more often than once every five seconds.

The test group lets a manager start a test. upsTestId names the test by an OBJECT IDENTIFIER, and setting it starts that test, with the set request rejected with an appropriate error if the test cannot be performed, including an attempt to start a test while another is in progress. A set to this object requires the presence of upsTestSpinLock in the same SNMP message, which stops two managers from starting tests at once. The results are reported in upsTestResultsSummary and upsTestResultsDetail, with the start time and elapsed time alongside. Five tests are well known: no tests initiated, abort the test in progress, the manufacturer's general systems test, a quick battery test, and a deep battery calibration, which puts the system on battery down to a manufacturer-set discharge level and leaves the battery in a low charge state needing time to recharge.

The control group is where a manager can act. upsShutdownType decides what a shutdown does, either turning off only the output or the whole system. upsShutdownAfterDelay, upsStartupAfterDelay and upsRebootWithDuration are all timed in seconds, and upsAutoRestart decides whether the system comes back by itself once the conditions that stopped it have been satisfied.
sections.plainLanguage: The alarm table is a live list of what is wrong right now, and the test and control groups let a manager run a battery check or ask the unit to shut down and restart on a timer, with a lock so that two managers cannot trip over each other.

sections.title: Configuration and Security
sections.content:
The configuration group holds the settings a manager may change. upsConfigInputVoltage is the nominal input voltage in RMS volts and upsConfigInputFreq the nominal input frequency in tenths of a hertz; on systems that support write access, a request to set a value that is not supported must be rejected with an appropriate error message, badValue for SNMPv1 or inconsistentValue for SNMPv2. The same pattern applies to upsConfigOutputVoltage and upsConfigOutputFreq, and the group also carries upsConfigOutputVA in volt-amps and upsConfigOutputPower in watts, the nominal ratings of the unit.

upsConfigLowBattTime is the value of upsEstimatedMinutesRemaining at which a low battery condition is declared, in minutes. For agents that support only discrete values the agent shall round up to the next supported value, and if the requested value is larger than the largest supported value then the largest supported value shall be selected. upsConfigAudibleStatus is an enumeration of disabled, enabled and muted, where muted temporarily silences an alarm that is sounding and the value reverts to enabled at the end of the period, while a write of muted when the alarm is not sounding is accepted but has no other effect. Finally upsConfigLowVoltageTransferPoint is the minimum input line voltage allowed before the UPS transfers to battery backup, and upsConfigHighVoltageTransferPoint the maximum, both in RMS volts.

The Security Considerations section is one sentence: security issues are not discussed in this memo. Several of the objects in this module are writable, and the memo does not say who may write them.
sections.plainLanguage: The settings cover the voltage and frequency the unit expects, how much power it is rated for, when to warn about a low battery, how loudly to complain, and at what voltage to switch to battery. The memo says nothing about who is allowed to change them.

viz.caption: THE OBJECT IDENTIFIER TREE OF THE UPS MIB
WHERE THE OUTPUT POWER IS COMING FROM

items.label: other
items.desc: None of the following.

items.label: none
items.desc: There is no source of output power, for example because the output breaker is open.

items.label: normal
items.desc: The output is taken from the normal path.

items.label: bypass
items.desc: The output is taken from the bypass path.

items.label: battery
items.desc: The output is coming from the batteries.

items.label: booster
items.desc: The output is taken from a booster path.

items.label: reducer
items.desc: The output is taken from a reducer path.

items.label: battery bad
items.desc: One or more batteries have been determined to require replacement.

items.label: on battery
items.desc: The UPS is drawing power from the batteries.

items.label: low battery
items.desc: The remaining battery run-time is less than or equal to upsConfigLowBattTime.

items.label: depleted battery
items.desc: The UPS will be unable to sustain the present load when and if the utility power is lost.

items.label: temperature bad
items.desc: A temperature is out of tolerance.

items.label: input bad
items.desc: An input condition is out of tolerance.

items.label: output bad
items.desc: An output condition, other than output overload, is out of tolerance.

items.label: output overload
items.desc: The output load exceeds the UPS output capacity.

items.label: on bypass
items.desc: The bypass is presently engaged on the UPS.

items.label: bypass bad
items.desc: The bypass is out of tolerance.

items.label: output off as requested
items.desc: The UPS has shut down as requested, that is, the output is off.

items.label: UPS off as requested
items.desc: The entire UPS has shut down as commanded.

items.label: charger failed
items.desc: An uncorrected problem has been detected within the UPS charger subsystem.

items.label: UPS output off
items.desc: The output of the UPS is in the off state.

items.label: UPS system off
items.desc: The UPS system is in the off state.

items.label: fan failure
items.desc: The failure of one or more fans in the UPS has been detected.

items.label: fuse failure
items.desc: The failure of one or more fuses has been detected.

items.label: general fault
items.desc: A general fault in the UPS has been detected.

items.label: diagnostic test failed
items.desc: The result of the last diagnostic test indicates a failure.

items.label: communications lost
items.desc: A problem has been encountered in the communications between the agent and the UPS.

items.label: awaiting power
items.desc: The UPS output is off and the UPS is awaiting the return of input power.

items.label: shutdown pending
items.desc: A upsShutdownAfterDelay countdown is underway.

items.label: shutdown imminent
items.desc: The UPS will turn off power to the load in less than 5 seconds.

items.label: test in progress
items.desc: A test is in progress, as initiated and indicated by the test group.
